title: LEGO Ideas 21373 Downton Abbey Revealed as Largest-Ever Ideas Set
summary: LEGO has confirmed 21373 Downton Abbey, a 4,711-piece recreation of Highclere Castle, as the biggest LEGO Ideas set by piece count yet — and it's got strong UK ties given the Hampshire filming location.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The Brothers Brick has published an early review of LEGO Ideas 21373 Downton Abbey, confirmed by LEGO Group as the largest LEGO Ideas set ever released by piece count, coming in at 4,711 pieces across 35 bags.

The set is based on a fan submission by Sebastian Veselka (known as BRO3 on LEGO Ideas), and recreates the Crawley family, their servants, and the Downton Abbey estate — filmed on location at the real Highclere Castle in Hampshire, England. LEGO Ideas designers Marina Stampoli (who also designed the previous record-holder, 21356 River Steamboat) and Jordan David Scott led the official build.

According to the review, the set includes a small sticker sheet (just 10 stickers) alongside a number of new minifigure prints, striking a balance between printed parts and stickers for a model of this scale.

Confirmed release details: the set launches October 1 for LEGO Insiders, and October 4 for everyone else, priced at £269.99 in the UK (US $349.99 / CAN $489.99).

## Why it matters
This is a milestone release for LEGO Ideas fans — the biggest set the theme has ever produced — and it has a genuine UK connection through its Highclere Castle inspiration. For collectors and display builders, it's set to be one of the standout large-scale builds of the year, and the fan-to-product journey (from Ideas submission to full release) is a great example of how community designs make it to shelves.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye out for the full Brothers Brick review as more details on the minifigure prints, hidden easter eggs on the stickers, and overall building experience are published ahead of the October 1 Insiders launch.

title: Fans plan to turn LEGO Downton Abbey into Wayne Manor

bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO Ideas set 21373 Downton Abbey, based on Highclere Castle, has caught the attention of Batman fans online. Communities such as the LEGO Batman subreddit have been discussing how the model's exterior could be reworked into Wayne Manor, with ideas floating around for reusing minifigures as Court of Owls members or Thomas and Martha Wayne.

This isn't an official LEGO product - it's a fan customisation idea, so treat any specific build plans as speculation from the community rather than confirmed projects.

Interestingly, there is a genuine design link worth noting. In a roundtable interview with Brick Fanatics and other LEGO fan media, set designer Marina Stampoli confirmed that colleagues at the LEGO Group asked if the model was actually a new Wayne Manor set while it was being developed. She said she researched the connection herself, noting that Highclere Castle's architecture bears a resemblance to Wollaton Hall in Nottingham, which was used as Wayne Manor in Christopher Nolan's Batman films.

## Why it matters
This is a great example of how a single official LEGO Ideas set can double as a base for entirely different custom builds. If you're into MOCs (my own creations) or display building, 21373 Downton Abbey could be a useful starting point for a superhero-themed project, even though it wasn't designed with Batman in mind.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye on fan forums and social media for any completed Wayne Manor MOCs built from this set, and watch for further LEGO Group comments on the coincidence, though there's no suggestion of an official Batman version being planned.

title: LEGO Downton Abbey: how Highclere Castle's real owners influenced the design
summary: LEGO designers reveal that the Earl and Countess of Carnarvon, whose real home inspired Downton Abbey, made specific requests that shaped the new 21373 set.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The LEGO Group has confirmed that the real-life owners of Highclere Castle, George and Fiona Herbert, the 8th Earl and Countess of Carnarvon, had direct input into the design of the new 21373 Downton Abbey set, due out on 1 October.

In a roundtable interview with fan media, LEGO Ideas Model Designer Marina Stampoli and Creative Lead Jordan David Scott explained that the Countess, known for her love of trees and her blog about life on the estate, asked for a tree to feature outside the house rather than the bench in the original fan design. The team added a tree for scale, while keeping it smaller than the real, much larger version so it wouldn't overshadow the castle itself.

The family also asked for a dog to be included, reflecting the real Labradors that roam the grounds. The finished set nods to this with a dog inspired by a scene from Season 6 of the show.

The 4,711-piece set recreates the fictional Yorkshire estate from Downton Abbey, even though Highclere Castle itself is actually in Hampshire.

## Why it matters
It's a nice example of how much real-world detail and personal input can go into a licensed LEGO Ideas set, especially one based on such a well-loved location and TV series. For collectors, it adds context and authenticity to what's already shaping up to be a major release for fans of detailed display builds.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye out for official images and reviews of 21373 Downton Abbey ahead of its 1 October release, which should reveal exactly how the tree and dog elements were finally realised in brick form.

title: LEGO Ideas: Wizard of Oz and RC Lens stadium projects reach 10,000 supporters
summary: Two new LEGO Ideas projects have hit the 10,000-supporter mark and will be considered in the third 2026 review round, including a Wizard of Oz diorama and a football stadium model.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Two more LEGO Ideas projects have reached the 10,000-supporter threshold needed to be considered in the platform's third 2026 review round.

The first is **The Wizard of Oz** by creator extraevancontent, their first submission to hit the milestone. It's a diorama featuring minifigures of the core cast and a full Yellow Brick Road leading to the Emerald City, based on the original 1939 film rather than the Wicked stage/film universe.

The second is **The Bollaert-Delelis Stadium** by Mirajane62, a joint project with their husband recreating the home ground of French football club RC Lens. Submitted in June, it took around four months to reach 10,000 supporters.

It's worth stressing that reaching 10,000 supporters only guarantees a project gets reviewed by the LEGO Group — it does not confirm a set will be released. Whether either idea becomes an actual product is entirely down to that review process, and there's no official confirmation of a set for either project at this stage.

## Why it matters
LEGO Ideas sets are one of the main routes for fan concepts to become official LEGO products, so reaching the review stage is a genuine milestone worth celebrating. For stadium fans, it's notable because the LEGO Group hasn't released a stadium model since 10299 Real Madrid – Santiago Bernabéu Stadium retired in 2023, so a positive review outcome here could mark a return for the theme. For Wizard of Oz fans, it offers a fresh take distinct from the existing Wicked-inspired Emerald City Wall Art set, which is itself due to retire later this year.

## What to watch next
Both projects now join others in the third 2026 LEGO Ideas review. Fans should watch for the official review results, which will determine whether either concept is greenlit for production as a real set.

title: Lumibricks' Christmas Pub takes aim at LEGO's Winter Village

bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Brick Fanatics has reviewed 15014 Christmas Pub, a new modular building from third-party construction toy brand Lumibricks, now available ahead of the festive season. The set comes in at 2,142 pieces and costs £116 / $156.99, and it's packed with extras: 32 built-in lights and a sound module offering six Christmas tunes, plus a USB Type-C port so you can upload your own music or messages.

According to the review, the set arrives in a hefty, premium-feeling box with two instruction manuals, a separate box for electronics, and multiple numbered bags — including dedicated bags for minifigures and fragile transparent pieces. The build itself was described as generally enjoyable, starting with ground floor plates and tiles before layering up. The reviewer praised the cosy design, clever lighting, and printed detail pieces, but flagged that some functions felt a bit pointless, the building experience was inconsistent in places, and the speaker only has one volume setting. Brick Fanatics scored it 7/10 overall, with an 8/10 for design and 9/10 for playability, but just 6/10 for minifigures.

Worth noting: this is a Lumibricks set, not an official LEGO Group product.

## Why it matters
For fans of festive modular builds and display sets, this shows compatible brick brands are stepping up their game with tech-heavy features like custom audio and dense lighting rigs — going beyond what's typically found in LEGO's own Winter Village Collection. It's a useful option to know about if you're building out a winter village display or just fancy something different this Christmas.

title: LEGO BrickLink Designer Program Series 9: what's changed from the original fan designs
summary: Final designs for the five BrickLink Designer Program Series 9 sets are in, and one build has been reworked far more than the rest. Crowdfunding opens 6 October 2026.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO has revealed the final designs and prices for the five BrickLink Designer Program Series 9 sets, showing how much each fan submission changed on its way to production. Crowdfunding for the series opens on 6 October 2026 at 8am PT / 4pm BST.

According to Brick Fanatics, changes across the range vary from barely noticeable to a full rework:

- **Fisherman's Village** (by Rocknbricks31) keeps the same layout and builds as the original pitch, with only minor colour swaps and reworked minifigures. Even the small hidden model "Easter eggs" are largely unchanged.
- **Sleepy Dragon Inn** (by MarinBD) has seen the biggest overhaul of the series. The minifigure line-up has been changed to focus on human characters across several LEGO Castle factions, moving away from the original's more varied fantasy cast. The inn's interior is mostly intact, but the banners have been expanded to represent four Castle factions, each carrying its own shield design. The set now leans much more into classic LEGO Castle territory than fantasy, and should sit well alongside sets like 21325 Medieval Castle or figures from 21348 Dungeons & Dragons: Red Dragon's Tale.
- **Wild West Blacksmith** (by llucky) has had the fewest changes of the three detailed so far, with the build staying largely the same and only minor tweaks made.

Details on the remaining two sets in the series weren't included in the available excerpt, so we'll update this once the full picture is confirmed.

## Why it matters
The BrickLink Designer Program is one of the few official routes for independent LEGO fan designers to see their creations produced and sold, and Series 9 shows just how much (or how little) LEGO's design team can reshape a winning pitch before it reaches shelves. For collectors and AFOLs, these before-and-after comparisons are a useful guide to what to expect when backing future rounds, and confirm which builds will pair naturally with existing Castle or fantasy-themed collections.

title: LEGO Shrek's Gingy minifigure may be prone to head cracks, fans report
summary: Some collectors say the Gingy minifigure from the new LEGO Shrek line has a tight-fitting head that could crack, and one fan has taken matters into his own hands with a craft knife.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
According to Brick Fanatics, the Gingy minifigure included in the new 71053 LEGO Shrek Minifigures series may share a design issue already seen on the Patrick Star minifigure from 11386 SpongeBob SquarePants: Bikini Bottom. Fans have spotted a line on the back of Gingy's head, and it's not yet confirmed whether this is simply a moulding mark or an actual crack caused by a tight fit between the head and neck peg.

Brick Fanatics says its own staffer tested this by wedging a small piece of paper into the line, which suggests it could genuinely be a crack rather than just a mould line - though this hasn't been officially confirmed by LEGO.

One member of the LEGO SHOWOFF Facebook group, Michael R. Burgio, says he used a craft knife to shave down part of the head peg to relieve the tightness and reduce the risk of cracking. Another fan, Tom Van Der Jeught, reportedly suggested sanding down the inside of the head instead. Both are unofficial, fan-made fixes and not something LEGO has recommended.

## Why it matters
Minifigure quality issues like this matter to collectors, especially for characters from a limited or sought-after wave. If confirmed as a genuine manufacturing fault, it could affect how confidently fans buy, display or trade Gingy figures - and whether LEGO addresses it in future production runs.

In the meantime, any at-home modifications like shaving or sanding pegs are unofficial fan fixes done at the collector's own risk, and could affect resale value or warranty-style goodwill replacements from LEGO customer service.

title: LEGO Downton Abbey becomes the biggest LEGO Ideas set ever, edging closer to the 5,000-piece cap
summary: The newly revealed 21373 Downton Abbey set weighs in at 4,711 pieces, making it the largest LEGO Ideas set to date and raising questions about whether the theme's piece limit could rise again.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO has officially revealed 21373 Downton Abbey, a 4,711-piece LEGO Ideas set due to release on 1 October. It's now the biggest LEGO Ideas set ever produced, and the closest any set in the theme has come to the current 5,000-piece cap on submissions.

That cap wasn't always so generous. Until September 2024, LEGO Ideas fan submissions were capped at 3,000 pieces, even though the LEGO Design Team often expanded projects well beyond that once they became official sets — think 21330 Home Alone (3,955 pieces), 21348 Dungeons & Dragons: Red Dragon's Tale (3,745 pieces), and 21323 Grand Piano (3,662 pieces). To keep pace with increasingly ambitious fan designs, LEGO raised the submission limit from 3,000 to 5,000 pieces.

Since then, sets have crept steadily closer to that new ceiling — 21356 River Steamboat was the first to break 4,000 pieces, and it shares a LEGO Model Designer (Marina Stampoli) with Downton Abbey.

In a roundtable interview with Brick Fanatics and other fan media, LEGO Ideas Creative Lead Jordan David Scott discussed the future of the piece limit, though no confirmed plans for a further increase have been announced.

## Why it matters
For LEGO Ideas fans and display builders, piece count often signals scale, detail and display presence. A set pushing right up against the 5,000-piece ceiling suggests fan designers are getting more ambitious — and hints that today's limit might not be the final word for the theme.

## What to watch next

title: LEGO Group plans giant Modular Buildings builds for 20th anniversary
summary: To mark 20 years of the Modular Buildings Collection, LEGO fan communities worldwide are building supersized versions of classic modulars using millions of pieces combined.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The LEGO Group is marking the 20th anniversary of its Modular Buildings Collection, which began with 10182 Café Corner in April 2007, by working with 22 Recognised LEGO Fan Communities from around the world.

Each community will design, engineer and build a giant-scale recreation of a classic modular, roughly four times the original size. Most builds will use around 500,000 LEGO elements each, with the two largest reaching closer to 750,000 pieces — bringing the total across all 22 builds to approximately 11.5 million elements.

While each community is responsible for its own model, all 22 builds are being coordinated so they form a cohesive overall collection. Once finished, they're expected to appear at major LEGO fan events and exhibitions through 2027 and into 2028, with some builds connected together where possible for larger combined displays.

It's not yet known which specific modular sets have been chosen for the giant treatment, and there's no confirmation that all 22 builds will ever be shown together at once.

## Why it matters
The Modular Buildings Collection is one of LEGO's most beloved AFOL (Adult Fan of LEGO) lines, and this project brings the global fan community together on a huge scale. For UK stadium and display builders, it's a great example of large-scale collaborative building techniques and could inspire similar community projects here.

## What to watch next
Expect further announcements confirming which modulars are being recreated, plus details on where and when the finished builds will be exhibited — UK fans should keep an eye out for any European event appearances in 2027–2028.

title: LEGO Shrek Minifigures: which one is hardest to find?

bodyMarkdown:

Because there's no way to tell which figure is inside without opening the bag, fans have been turning to the Brick Search app, which uses its minifigure code scanner to read the data matrix code on each figure's base and match it against a database.

It's worth flagging that this is scan data from Brick Search's own user base rather than official figures from LEGO, so it reflects a sample rather than confirmed production ratios.

## Why it matters
Blind-bag minifigure lines are always a bit of a lottery, and data like this gives collectors a useful (if unofficial) steer on which characters might take longer to find - handy if you're chasing a full set or specific favourites like Puss in Boots.

## What to watch next
As more figures get scanned over the coming weeks, the percentages could shift, so it's worth treating this as an early snapshot rather than a final verdict on rarity.
